item.title: Scaling Lean Theorem Proving for Real-World Code Verification
item.dc:creator: Debargha Ganguly, Divya Raghunathan, Dejan Jovanović, Vikash Singh, Soonho Kong, Aaron Tomb, Aman Goel, Ferhat Erata, Sam Bayless
item.description:
Builds an agentic Lean prover with a stateless Lean elaboration service, and generates Lean verification tasks from Rust code translated with Aeneas.
We present EasyProver, a Lean proving system built from recursive agents with isolated contexts, asynchronous search, parallel tactic probing, and an elastic elaboration service. Using an off-the-shelf frontier model with no additional training, it proves 669/672 PutnamBench problems and all six IMO 2026 formalizations and resolves 597/600 NTP4VC verification conditions and all 189 VERINA tasks by proof or refutation. Because these benchmarks are close to saturation, we also introduce Aegis, which converts competitive programming problems into much harder verification tasks over real implementations. The pipeline writes safe Rust solutions, translates them into Lean with Aeneas, generates specifications, and labels each frozen statement with a kernel-checked proof or refutation. It produces 2,045 differentially validated Rust-Lean program pairs and 11,533 candidate specifications. Unlike hand-written benchmarks, these tasks carry implementation-level obligations from fixed-width arithmetic, explicit failure, generated loops, casts, and functionalized mutation. On a stratified sample of 2,000 statements, EasyProver proves 1,054 (52.7%) within a 30-minute budget per statement. The same tasks can also be used to benchmark other provers and as rewards for reinforcement learning.

item.title: Random Centres and the $\varepsilon$-Dependence of Constant-Round Planar Domination
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Senge
item.description:
Key lemmas, level bounds, exponent estimates and the path lower bound are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib, in a public repository.
It was recently shown (arXiv:2610.09618) that the infimum of the approximation ratios of deterministic constant-round LOCAL algorithms for minimum dominating set on planar graphs is 7. The $(7+\varepsilon)$-approximation given there runs in $T_0+O((c_0/\varepsilon)^κ)$ rounds with $κ=\ln 3/\ln(24/23)\approx 25.81$, and it is asked there whether this exponent can be substantially reduced. We replace the heaviest-edge star selection in its clustering step by a random-centre rule: every part becomes a centre independently with probability $p$, and every non-centre joins its heaviest centre neighbour. For planar graphs this gives $κ<5.89$ with $p=3/8$ (three fair coins per part and level) and $κ<6.7$ with $p=1/2$. An analysis that counts only the join edges cannot go below $5.74$. For every proper minor-closed class of density $a$, the new exponent is never worse, and with about $\frac12\log_2 a$ fair coins per part and level it is smaller by a factor that tends to $8$ as the density grows. This is optimal for the rule when $a$ is an integer and the class contains all $K_{a,n}$. The planar bounds hold verbatim on the torus, the projective plane and the Klein bottle. We then turn to the dependence on $\varepsilon$. On paths, every deterministic $r$-round algorithm for fractional domination, and every randomized one that always outputs a dominating set, has (expected) ratio at least $1+1/(r+4)$. So these approximations need $Ω(1/\varepsilon)$ rounds on every minor-closed class that contains all paths, and on paths this is tight up to an additive constant. On forests and on outerplanar graphs, with no bound on the degree, $O(1/\varepsilon)$ rounds suffice, so there the optimal number of rounds is $Θ(1/\varepsilon)$. The planar level bounds, the bounds on paths and the deterministic bound on forests are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib.

item.title: Hierarchical Laminates Cannot Reproduce All Effective Properties of Planar Two-Phase Composites: A Counterexample with a 16-Component Potential
item.dc:creator: Lianghao Cao
item.description:
The main counterexample theorem and the two-well envelope gap are formally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib, using only standard axioms.
Designing a composite requires understanding which effective properties can be achieved through varying its microstructure, i.e., the spatial arrangement of given constituent materials. Hierarchical laminates, created by successive layering, reach many known limits on these properties, making it natural to ask whether they can reproduce every effective response obtainable from the same constituents. We answer this question negatively for planar two-phase composites governed by linear systems whose potentials have 16 or more components. We construct constituent material properties and, at any prescribed nontrivial phase fraction, periodic microstructures whose effective properties cannot be approximated by hierarchical laminates, even when layer directions, proportions, and the number of layering steps are unrestricted. We design the constituents so that all hierarchical laminates have equal effective energies at two prescribed mean gradients. The key step is to construct a medium whose local properties are those of horizontal laminates with smoothly varying phase fractions, but whose effective energies violate this equality. Approximating these energies with sufficiently fine periodic stripes of the original constituents yields the two-phase counterexample. This construction also gives a negative answer to the two-well relaxation problem: the minimum of two positive-definite homogeneous quadratic forms on $\mathbb{R}^{2\times32}$ can have distinct quasiconvex and rank-one convex envelopes. The counterexample and the strict inequality between the envelopes are formally verified in Lean 4.

item.title: OpenFrontiers: A Collection of Open Research Problems and a Benchmark for Scientific Rediscovery
item.dc:creator: Jiarui Yao, Ruida Wang, Tong Zhang
item.description:
Benchmark of 200 research-level math problems with checked Lean 4 statements; LLM agent proofs are graded by two independent Lean checkers with Mathlib.
Large language models (LLMs) have shown increasing promise in research-level problem solving, yet a comprehensive collection of such problems is still missing, and evaluating them on research-level problems remains challenging. We introduce OpenFrontiers, a cross-disciplinary resource that combines a structured corpus of open research problems with a retrospective benchmark of recently resolved problems in mathematics. The corpus records problem statements, context, progress, and other information for 12,151 problems. The benchmark contains 200 problems, 110 resolved in 2026 and 90 still open, each with a Lean 4 statement checked by automated probes and two independent reviews; a subset HQ-50 further filters based on quality score, etc. Our evaluation protocol grades formal proofs with two independent checkers in an isolated sandbox under closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web conditions. Evaluating seven LLM agents on the HQ-50 subset under a standardized budget, we find that closed-book rediscovery is rare, at most 7 of 40 resolved problems, whereas live-web success mostly reflects retrieval of published solutions. By linking a broad research-problem corpus to a formally graded evaluation subset with documented solutions, OpenFrontiers provides a foundation for measuring research-level rediscovery and studying progress toward solving currently open scientific problems. The dataset and benchmark could be found in https://huggingface.co/collections/FlippyDora/openfrontiers.

item.title: The lower tail of triangle counts in sparse random graphs
item.dc:creator: Dong Huang, Shuangping Li
item.description:
The authors formalized the paper's arguments on the lower-tail graphon variational problem in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with parts written by AI models.
Let $T_n$ be the number of triangles in the Erdős-Rényi random graph $G(n,p)$ with $n^{-1/2}\ll p\ll1$ and fix $η\in(0,1)$. We study the large deviation rate of the lower tail event $T_n\leη\mathbb{E}[T_n]$, and the typical structure of $G(n,p)$ conditioned on this event. By earlier work [16,19,21,49], both the rate and the structure are governed by a variational problem over graphons. In this work we solve this variational problem for every $η\in(0,1)$. We show that every minimizer is either a constant graphon or a step graphon with two blocks of equal size. Correspondingly, the conditioned graph is close to an Erdős-Rényi graph or to a symmetric stochastic block model with two blocks. These two regimes are separated by a first order phase transition at the threshold $η_*=0.009217\ldots$. This resolves a conjecture of Zhao [78] and an open problem of Janson and Warnke [39] on triangles. It thereby gives a complete description of the lower tail of triangle counts in this range of $p$.

item.title: A counterexample to Tokareva's conjecture on sums of two bent functions
item.dc:creator: Yansong Feng, Hao Jiang, Guancheng Li, Tianyi Li, Lili Tang
item.description:
The main counterexample theorems (Theorem 4.2 and Theorem 4.7) on sums of two bent functions are formally verified in Lean 4.
It is well known that the sum of two bent functions on $\mathbb{F}^n$ has algebraic degree at most $n/2$ for even $n\ge 4$. Tokareva conjectured that the converse holds: every Boolean function with degree at most $n/2$ can be written as a sum of two bent functions. The conjecture has been verified for even $n\leq 6$ and for several special classes of Boolean functions. We disprove this conjecture by showing that $x_1x_2(x_3x_4+x_5x_6+x_7x_8)$ is not a sum of two bent functions on $\mathbb{F}^8$. We extend this construction to obtain counterexamples in every even dimension $n\ge 8$. Using Shaporenko's reduction, we also obtain explicit counterexamples to Tokareva's derivative conjecture in every even dimension $n\ge 10$.

item.title: Bijective Non-Contractive Maps of Hereditarily Precompact Quasi-Metric Spaces Need Not Be Isometries
item.dc:creator: Thomas Duzer
item.description:
The core counterexample construction, including quasi-metric axioms, hereditary precompactness, and the circle instance, is formalized sorry-free in Lean 4 over Mathlib.
Zavarzina asked whether every bijective non-contractive self-map of a precompact quasi-metric space is an isometry. We answer the question in the negative, in a stronger form: on a hereditarily precompact quasi-metric space (a tolled extension of the irrational rotation over Z), the shift is a bijective non-contractive map that is not an isometry. The construction generalizes: for every metric space Y, every bijective isometry $σ$ of Y, and every point whose $σ$-orbit is aperiodic and totally bounded, the tolled Z-extension is such a counterexample; instances include the irrational rotation and the p-adic odometer. The conjugate space is not precompact, so the two-sided hypothesis of Zavarzina's positive result is sharp, and the space is not expand-contract plastic. The core results, including the general scheme and the circle instance, are machine-checked in Lean 4 over mathlib, sorry-free (no unproved steps), under a pinned toolchain. A structural section proves a monochromy theorem: for every strict pair on a hereditarily precompact space, one endpoint's backward self-returns have self-defect at least a quarter of the pair's defect, uniformly on a chain-closed displacement set. Boundary results delimit what remains open: one-sided compactness together with separation.

item.title: Exact distances and measurement allocation for logical Pauli readout
item.dc:creator: Shuoming An, Fusheng Yang
item.description:
Lean certifies finite distance values, algebraic and finite-code results, and five arithmetic resource-count lemmas; the formal development is archived on Zenodo.
The minimum fault weight of a logical readout depends jointly on data-error persistence, check redundancy and time-boundary constraints. For any binary check matrix $H$ and nonzero parity support $w$, we prove that a repeated-readout model with a zero-syndrome endpoint has exact distance $\min_{w\cdot y=1}[\operatorname{wt}(y)+q\operatorname{wt}(Hy)]$ for at least $q$ wrong readouts. This reduces the search over fault histories to one weighted spatial minimum and gives the minimum repetition count for each adjacent-column check in square Bacon–Shor and generalized Shor readouts. Combining those checks with redundant Gauss-check pair products yields an exact joint distance and an outcome-count optimum within the specified gauged-readout family. At target distance $m$, one round uses $m^2$ outcomes, compared with $m(2m-1)$ for the repeated baseline in the same phenomenological model. For a one-epoch bare-ancilla CNOT implementation, we prove a schedule-dependent distance upper bound by constructing an accepted wrong readout from one gate fault and outcome flips. The bound identifies necessary timing conditions for retaining the target distance and gives matching upper bounds of three for the best tested schedules at both $m=3$ and $m=5$.

item.title: CLAD: Constrained Abstract Domain for Neural Network Verification
item.dc:creator: Hai Duong, Thanh Le, ThanhVu Nguyen
item.description:
Soundness (weak duality) and tightness (strong duality via Sion's minimax theorem) of the CLAD bounds are mechanized sorry-free in Lean 4 with Mathlib.
Neural network verification (NNV) formally verifies that a network satisfies a specified property for all inputs within a defined region. Modern NNV tools employ abstract domains to compute a sound over-approximation of the network's behavior from the given input region, thus the tightness of these abstractions essentially determines efficiency. A long line of increasingly precise domains has been developed, but they all describe the valid input region in the same restrictive way, e.g., an Lp-norm ball. A practical input region is rarely a simple Lp ball, but rather a combination Lp ball with additional constraints. Verifying a network over such a region with existing abstraction produces a loose over-approximation, which results in either failing to verify a property or spurious counterexamples. We introduce Constrained Lagrangian Abstract Domain (CLAD), a new abstract domain that computes a sound over-approximation of neural networks over input regions defined by a combination of convex constraints. CLAD propagates these constraints and tightens bounds over the true feasible region. However, bounding a neuron over the intersection of these constraints has no closed-form solution, so CLAD relaxes each constraint into the objective with a Lagrange multiplier and solves the resulting max-min problem with a projected primal-dual method, alternating a projected gradient step on the input with a multiplier update. CLAD supports any convex constraint with a subgradient, e.g., from automatic differentiation. We evaluate CLAD on 1,944 instances across four convolutional networks with motion-blur structured perturbations with halfspace or L2-ball constraints. On standard unconstrained Linf property, CLAD verifies as many instances as GCPCROWN at a similar runtime. On constrained properties, CLAD verifies 60% more instances than GCPCROWN on L2-ball properties, and 22% more in total.

item.title: Approximate Counting for Mixed $p$-Spin Glasses in Weak External Fields via Cluster Expansion
item.dc:creator: Qiang Wu
item.description:
The authors developed a companion Lean formalization of the work, assisted by Codex and posted on GitHub.
We give algorithms for approximating the partition function $Z_N$ of the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick (SK) model and finite mixed Ising $p$-spin models with $p\ge 3$. The algorithms apply at a fixed margin below the second-moment threshold $β_{\mathrm f}$ with homogeneous weak external fields $|h|\leqρ_0N^{-1/4}$, for fixed $ρ_0>0$. For any accuracy $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and failure parameter $δ\in(0,1)$, they approximate $\log Z_N$ to additive error $\varepsilon$. The number of exact operations is polynomial jointly in $N$, $\varepsilon^{-1}$, and $δ^{-1}$. The disorder variables have i.i.d symmetric distribution with unit variance. The failure probability is at most $δ$ plus an explicit disorder tail bound. This tail bound tends to zero under a finite fourth moment condition. Our approach builds on the cluster expansions of Aizenman–Lebowitz–Ruelle \cite{ALR87} and Dey–Wu \cites{DW23,DW26}. For higher-order mixtures, we retain hypergraphs using few vertices and evaluate their total weight deterministically through local spin averages and inclusion–exclusion. For SK, we impose cutoffs on the number of vertices of degree at least three and on the total number of edges. We estimate the retained sum using randomized color coding \cite{AYZ95}. A lower tail control based on reverse hypercontractivity \cite{MOS13} converts the mean-square approximation of the normalized partition function into logarithmic accuracy.

item.title: Algebraic Completeness of Feynman Premeasures: The Henstock-Kurzweil Path Integral and Operator Wick Calculus in Lean 4
item.dc:creator: Yu. N. Berdinsky
item.description:
Formalizes in Lean 4 on Mathlib the Henstock–Kurzweil free-field Feynman integral, the Fresnel formula, the generating functional and Wick's theorem, with no sorry and no new axioms.
We formalize in Lean 4 the gauge closure of the Feynman functional integral for the free field without Wick rotation. First, the restriction to box divisions is removed via a direction bound and a uniform Riemann-sum estimate for all $δ$-fine cylindrical divisions. Second, the coordinate measure on $\mathbb{R}^k$ is identified with the standard Gaussian one. Third, the Saks-Henstock lemma and additivity are proved. Fourth, the Fresnel formula $\int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{i a x^2/2} dx = \sqrt{2π/a} e^{iπ/4}$ is proved as an improper (gauge) integral. This yields the projective consistency of the oscillating Gaussian premeasure and the existence of the free-field integral. The free field is completely closed: we prove the Fresnel formula for an arbitrary symmetric positive-definite action $A$, compute the generating functional and the two-point function $\langle y_p y_q \rangle = i(A^{-1})_{pq}$, and prove Wick's theorem. The interacting field $λ\varphi^4$, unbounded generators, and renormalisation remain open. All results are machine-verified with no sorry or new axioms.

item.title: Linear-Time FPT Rectilinear Planarity Testing of Series-Parallel Graphs
item.dc:creator: Giacomo Ortali
item.description:
Key Lemma, piece-count bounds, algorithm correctness and fixed-root cost are formalized in a single sorry-free Lean 4 file using Mathlib.
A planar graph is rectilinear planar if it admits a planar orthogonal drawing without bends. For series-parallel graphs in the variable embedding setting the best known testing algorithm takes $O(n^2)$ time. We show that rectilinear planarity of a series-parallel graph with maximum degree four can be tested in $2^{O(k)}\cdot n$ time, where $k$ is the number of degree-4 vertices; the planar embedding is not fixed. In particular, the running time is subquadratic when $k=o(\log n)$. Each node of the SPQ$^*$-tree stores the set of its admissible spiralities; we show that this set is a union of $2^{O(k)}$ arithmetic progressions of step two. All proofs are in the paper and are additionally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib.

item.title: Counting the Fixed Points of Binary Belief Propagation: Generic Degree, Syzygies, and Real Solutions
item.dc:creator: Yusuke Watanabe
item.description:
Main theorems on the generic BP degree, edge-incidence ring resolutions, and minimum real fixed-point counts are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with Lean source released.
How many fixed points does belief propagation have on a binary pairwise model? Over complex parameters, the admissible equations of a finite loopless multigraph form an algebraic family whose generic degree we determine: it is a graph state sum over edge sets without vertices of degree one, each vertex of positive degree contributing one less than its degree. We give two geometric realizations of this state sum. The first is the total Betti number of a universal edge-incidence ring constructed without parameters. Its full graded Betti table is the state sum, its Tor algebra is natural for noncontracting graph maps, the alternating numerator recovers the graph polynomial of Watanabe and Fukumizu, and an Artin reduction by a regular sequence realizes the one-variable specialization, corrected for tree components. The second lies in the actual family: at the strong-field boundary each state factor is a ramification index, and at sufficiently strong field the state charts exhaust the admissible complex fiber. For fixed nonzero real couplings, every Eulerian message-sign sector contains a real fixed point at every external field, and strong fields attain this lower bound: one admissible real fixed point per element of the binary cycle space and one positive fixed point. For graphs of maximum degree at most three, this minimum equals the number of minimal module generators of the edge-incidence ring. One state decomposition connects the complex degree, graded syzygies, and an attained minimum real count. The degree, selected ring and resolution statements, and the real counts are formalized in Lean 4.

item.title: Depositing More Should Not Earn Less: Supplier Income Monotonicity and Rate Curve Design in Pooled Lending Markets
item.dc:creator: Ahzam Khan, Cavey Cool
item.description:
Most of the paper's results on supplier income monotonicity and admissible rate curves are formalized in a Lean 4 library, released with a coverage record.
In utilization dependent interest rate models, adding liquidity can reduce a supplier's total interest income even as the supplier's balance increases. A supplier holding a fraction $α$ of final pool supply keeps income nondecreasing with a marginal deposit exactly when $α(1+η)\leq1$, where $η$ is the elasticity of the borrow rate with respect to utilization. When the condition fails, the supplier can instead raise its income by withdrawing, which pushes utilization further up. On two public Drift markets, a lender held more of the pool than the curve protected in at least one hour in nine on SOL and one in thirteen on USDC. A protocol turns this into a design constraint by choosing, at each utilization, the largest supplier share it intends to protect. That choice caps the elasticity, and integrating the cap describes every admissible curve. Protecting the same share at every utilization gives a power law boundary, and protecting every fresh depositor gives a hyperbolic one. On a multiple kink USDT market, compliant repairs can lower or raise supplier income, because the constraint governs how income responds to a deposit and not the price level.

item.title: An upper bound of 61 for the Ramsey number $R(3,3,3,3)$
item.dc:creator: Milos Tatarevic
item.description:
Lean 4 formalizes the combinatorial reductions to 56,723 SAT formulas, checks the template-classification certificates, and emits the CNF formulas. The SAT refutations themselves are an unverified premise.
We improve the upper bound on the classical Ramsey number $R(3,3,3,3)$ from 62 to 61. The proof is based on a global incidence count, classifications of small neighborhoods and exhaustive SAT computations. We formalize the mathematical reductions in Lean and refute every resulting formula with two SAT solvers.

item.title: Resolvent Components of Completely Normal Elements and the Morgan-Mullen Conjecture
item.dc:creator: Florian Hellwig
item.description:
The proof of the Morgan–Mullen conjecture for n>q and two corollaries, including all computer-assisted steps, is formalised in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with two cited results as axioms.
We study completely normal elements of $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$, that is, elements that are normal over every intermediate field, through partial Lagrange resolvents. In these coordinates, complete normality splits into independent components, in a way closely related to Hachenberger's decomposition theory. Our main tool is a structure theorem for the components; together with a finite computation, it shows that every component has weight (the sum of the probabilities that its conditions fail) at most $3/4$, uniformly in $n$. Combined with the classical character-sum method, this gives an explicit sufficient criterion for the existence of a primitive completely normal element. We verify the criterion for all $n>q$ except $70$ pairs $(q,n)$, which we settle with explicit elements found by computer. Since the case $n\le q$ is due to Garefalakis and Kapetanakis, this confirms the conjecture of Morgan and Mullen (1996) that every $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ contains a primitive element that is completely normal over $\mathbb{F}_q$. The same estimates give two further results. First, Hachenberger's conjectured lower bound $(q-1)^{n'}q^{(p^a-1)n'}$ for the number of completely normal elements, where $p$ is the characteristic and $n=p^an'$ with $p\nmid n'$, holds for all pairs $(q,n)$; it was known for regular pairs. Second, primitivity and complete normality are asymptotically independent: as $q^n\to\infty$, the number of primitive completely normal elements is $(1+o(1))\,\varphi(q^n-1)/(q^n-1)$ times the number of completely normal elements (for fixed $n$ this was known). Our arguments for $n>q$ and for both further results, including every computer-assisted step, are formalised in Lean 4 with Mathlib; the formalisation takes the case $n\le q$ and an explicit bound of Rosser and Schoenfeld as axioms and relies on Lean's compiler and interpreter for the large computations.

item.title: Counting by the Book: Verifying Alaska's Ranked-Choice Elections
item.dc:creator: Lucy Horowitz
item.description:
Formalizes Alaska's ranked-choice tabulation statute in Lean 4, proves a tabulator implementation correct against the specification, and kernel-checks the tabulation results of 115 contests.
We present Alaska's ranked-choice elections as a case study in Formally Verified Democracy, a program to establish election results through formally checked proofs. We formalize an interpretation of Alaska's tabulation rules in Lean, verify its implementation, and prove election-specific results. Across 115 ranked-choice contests in Alaska since 2022, we identify 75 ballot records across 10 contests that were counted differently from this interpretation by a program reproducing the published results, without changing any winners. We trace these differences to overvotes and duplicate rankings and examine their legal justification, showing how formal verification can expose consequential choices in translating election law into software.

item.title: Automatic Certified Differentiation in Lean
item.dc:creator: Ramy Shahin
item.description:
Implements certified automatic differentiation via Lean metaprogramming, composing Mathlib derivative theorems into step-wise correctness certificates.
Automatic differentiation (the automatic computation of numerical function derivatives) has many applications, especially in scientific computing and machine learning. Several approaches to automate the calculation of derivatives have been presented. Common challenges facing those approaches include (1) having to define derivative rules for different classes of functions, (2) having to manipulate program symbols to understand the semantics of the function being differentiated, and construct the derivative function, and (3), more importantly, ensuring that the calculated derivative is correct. In this paper, we present an approach for automatic certified differentiation using the Lean proof assistant. By certified, we mean a correctness certificate is computed together with the derivative function and a domain on which the derivative is guaranteed to be valid. Our approach leverages existing derivative theorems included in the Mathlib Lean library instead of having to define our own rules. We also utilize Lean metaprogramming to manipulate the symbolic structure of the input function, and to construct the derivative function. The correctness certificate is computed step-wise as we apply Mathlib theorems. To make the search efficient, we index the derivative theorems by the function they differentiate. We evaluate our approach on 500 randomly generated functions: with the index, all of them are differentiated, with a median time of 0.18\,s per function, 8.6 times faster than without the index.

item.title: Reasoning about the Genetic Code in Lean
item.dc:creator: Colin T. Jones, Tyler R. Josephson
item.description:
Formalizes transcription, translation, replication and mutation in Lean 4 with Mathlib, proving redundancy and injectivity properties of the genetic code.
The genetic code exhibits redundancy, meaning that multiple distinct nucleotide sequences can encode the same amino acid sequence, a property mathematically characterized as non-injectivity. While this phenomenon is well studied in molecular biology, its rigorous verification within a computational framework remains limited. In this work, we present a machine-verified model of the central dogma of molecular biology using the Lean 4 interactive theorem prover. We formalize nucleic acid bases and amino acids as inductive types and define transcription and translation as functions mapping DNA sequences to RNA and subsequently to polypeptides. Within this framework, we prove key properties of these biological processes, including the redundancy of the genetic code, injectivity of transcription, and the non-injectivity of translation. Additionally, we formalize auxiliary processes such as DNA replication and mutation, and verify properties such as length conservation under transcription and point mutations. Finally, we demonstrate how Lean 4 helps prevent semantic errors in our code, showing its effectiveness as a tool for advancing reliable, bug-free scientific computing, particularly within the life sciences.

item.title: How Stable Are LLM-Generated Proofs Under Program Refactoring? A Stress Test for Verifiable Code Generation
item.dc:creator: Aravind Mandiga, Guoming Li
item.description:
Builds a benchmark of Lean-certified behavior-preserving refactorings of VERINA tasks and re-checks fixed Lean proofs against them to measure proof survival.
Benchmarks for verifiable code generation usually test a proof against one fixed implementation. We ask whether the same proof remains valid after a program refactoring that preserves behavior. We introduce RefactorProof, which derives 458 Lean-certified variants from the 185 VERINA tasks that compile in our pinned environment while holding the specification and evaluated proof fixed byte-for-byte. VERINA supplies reference proofs for 46 tasks, all from its basic split; the primary model-versus-reference comparisons further match on 21-25 short, non-recursive tasks. Structural refactorings expose substantial brittleness across proof sources: task-normalized structural PSR is 4.3% for the supplied references and 13.3-26.8% for the specialized provers. On the matched tasks, specialized prover proofs nevertheless have higher overall unchanged-proof survival than the supplied reference artifacts: +15.6 points for DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B, +18.8 for Goedel-Prover-V2-32B, and +20.3 for Goedel-Prover-V2-8B; all three 95% CIs exclude zero. The ordering persists after excluding universally survived T1 variants, under family-balanced aggregation, and under alternative deployable valid-proof selection rules. However, unchanged-proof failure is not the same as high repair cost: predefined one-identifier edits repair 51/54 eligible reference structural failures and 58/85 eligible prover failures. RefactorProof therefore measures unchanged-proof stability under program refactoring, not the cost of maintaining a proof after it breaks.

item.title: count-catcher: Lean Theorems from Model Counting Certificates
item.dc:creator: Johannes K. Fichte, Stefan Szeider
item.description:
Builds a Lean tool that checks CPOG model-counting certificates in Lean, yielding verified count theorems combined with Mathlib results such as Burnside's lemma.
We present count-catcher, a tool that turns a CPOG certificate of a count by the exact model counter d4 into a Lean theorem that a CNF formula defined in Lean has exactly N models over V variables. With an encoding lemma, this theorem becomes a theorem about the number of combinatorial objects. A CPOG certificate consists of a Boolean circuit equivalent to the formula and a proof of equivalence. count-catcher checks in Lean that the formula implies the circuit (forward check) and the circuit implies the formula (reverse check). For the forward check, lrat-catcher streams a refutation through the LRAT checker of Lean's standard library. The reverse check and the validity check of the circuit are computations proved correct in Lean. Lean runs all three checks as compiled code, so the theorem depends on Lean's kernel, compiler and runtime, as does CPOG's verified checker. We combine the theorem with results from Mathlib, for instance with Burnside's lemma to count graphs up to isomorphism. We prove the number of Latin squares of order 8 as a weighted sum of hundreds of certified counts from about eight terabytes of certificates. We turn about half of the 2022 Model Counting Competition formulas into theorems, with the three checks taking about a quarter of the time of CPOG's verified checker. We found that CPOG's unverified checker reported wrong counts, and removed its verified checker's dependence on two unproved lemmas. End to end, a theorem costs about the same as a checked count.

item.title: h1: A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving
item.dc:creator: Skander Moalla, Ahmad Rammal, Niket Patel, Remi Munos, Julia Kempe
item.description:
Builds h1, an agentic harness giving LLMs an efficient Lean 4/Mathlib interface, evaluated on Lean benchmarks and used to settle open FormalConjectures problems.
While progress in informal mathematics has come largely from scaling the chain-of-thought and agentic reasoning of frontier language models, formal theorem proving has increasingly relied on human-designed workflows around these models, such as planning, decomposition, and orchestrating specialized provers. This raises a bitter-lesson question: can a simple agentic loop that scales test-time compute match these workflows? The answer matters as formal verification must scale to keep up with frontier models producing research mathematics, yet new workflows rarely settle it, as their gains are often confounded with stronger models or more compute. We study this question with h1, a simple harness that gives a model an efficient interface to Lean 4 and keeps it working through verifier feedback and self-reflection, without imposing a decomposition or search structure. h1 reaches state-of-the-art results on PutnamBench, FATE-X, and FormalConjectures100-Solved, settles eight open problems in FormalConjectures, and, at matched models, matches or outperforms specialized workflows such as Goedel-Architect and AlphaProof Nexus, surprisingly showing that a single attempt (pass@1) can often scale to solve open problems. Through ablations and matched-model comparisons with Claude Code and AxProverBase, we find that simplicity alone is not enough: an efficient Lean interface largely determines cost and solve rate. We thus recommend that future work evaluate frontier models with efficient execution feedback before prescribing workflows, at the risk of bitter lessons.

item.title: Conditional Stable Laws and Rare-Event Limits for Absorbing Markov Chains
item.dc:creator: Bernat Bassols Cornudella, Matheus M Castro
item.description:
Main theorems A–F and nine remarks on conditional limit laws for absorbing Markov chains are formalised in Lean 4 using Mathlib.
We establish conditional limit theorems, pointwise in the initial state, for absorbing Markov chains on a compact metric space $M$. We assume $L^1(M,ρ)$-continuous transition densities, irreducibility and aperiodicity. For the observable $f_β(x)=d_M(x,x_0)^{-β}$, with suitable $x_0$ satisfying $ρ(B_r(x_0))\sim C_d(x_0)r^d$, we prove that the point-process of normalised observations converges to a Poisson random measure. This yields totally right-skewed $α$-stable laws for $α=d/β\in(0,2)$ and, at the boundary value $α=2$, a Gaussian limit with the non-standard normalisation $\sqrt{n\log n}$. We also establish a conditional central limit theorem for $L^2$ observables, exponential deviation bounds for bounded observables and a conditional Poisson law for visits to shrinking targets. The results and remarks have been formalised in Lean 4.

item.title: Parabolic Rectifiable Reifenberg for Measures
item.dc:creator: Robert Koirala
item.description:
All theorems, corollaries and a key example are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib ( 176k lines), checked against a Mathlib-only specification via Comparator and nanoda.
We announce a structure theory for measures on $\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}$ equipped with the parabolic distance. Our results include a parabolic rectifiable Reifenberg theorem for arbitrary Radon measures, qualitative and quantitative characterizations of regular parabolic rectifiability by Jones square functions, and sharp results for $L^p$ beta numbers. The results hold in every parabolic dimension and extend the theories of Edelen–Naber–Valtorta, Azzam–Tolsa and David–Semmes to space-time. The stated theorems and corollaries, together with their proofs, are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib.

item.title: Persistence Pays: Square-root condition-number dependence for Metropolis-adjusted kinetic Langevin Monte Carlo with a non-reversibly updated accept/reject uniform
item.dc:creator: Nawaf Bou-Rabee
item.description:
Main theorems and key propositions, with their supporting definitions, are formalized and checked in Lean 4 against Mathlib; sources are in a public repository.
We prove accelerated mixing for a Metropolis-adjusted kinetic Langevin sampler: the OBABO splitting with friction $2\sqrt m$, adjusted with Neal's non-reversibly updated uniform, which is redrawn after every epoch of $E$ steps. For targets $e^{-U}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $mI\preceq\nabla^2U\preceq LI$ and an $L_H$-Lipschitz Hessian, started from a Gaussian at an approximate minimizer, the chain reaches total variation accuracy $\varepsilon$ after $\tilde O\big(\sqrt{κd}+\sqrt{L_H}(d/m)^{3/4}\big)$ gradient evaluations, where $κ=L/m$ and $\tilde O$ hides logarithmic factors. The $\sqrtκ$ term is necessary, already on Gaussian targets. The proof discretizes Lu's entropic hypocoercivity by means of an entropy inequality for free transport, so that the relative entropy of the unadjusted chain decays at a rate of order $\sqrt m$ up to a discretization bias. With the non-reversibly updated uniform, the leading energy errors of velocity Verlet telescope along a path. A coupling argument combines the two. On Bayesian logistic regression posteriors for two standard data sets, which satisfy these assumptions, the gradient cost of the chain with the non-reversibly updated uniform grows roughly like the square root of the condition number at the posterior mode, and that of standard adjusted OBABO roughly like its $3/4$ power.

item.title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
item.dc:creator: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
item.description:
Language model agents translate statistics papers' statements and proofs into Lean 4 with Mathlib, which then checks each result along the paper's own route.
Papers in statistical theory rest on long proofs that few readers check line by line. We present KAPPA (Kit of Agents for Proof-checking Papers with a proof Assistant), open-source software that organizes language model agents, run by Claude Code, to translate the proofs of a LaTeX paper into the proof assistant Lean 4 with its library Mathlib and check them there, result by result. Each numbered result receives one of four verdicts: verified unconditionally; verified conditionally, with every cited or unproved input stated as a named hypothesis; issue recorded, with its place in the paper and the side at fault; or unfinished, with the reason. The kit follows the paper's own proof step by step, rather than finding a new one. Separate agents write and review, each statement is compared with the paper before it is proved and fingerprinted afterwards, and every verdict rests on evidence that can be rerun without a language model. The kit runs unattended for hours, waits out usage limits, re-checks only what a revision changed and reports its cost by role, model and result. We describe the design, walk through a complete run, and apply the kit to four example papers with answer keys and to three published statistical papers, checked blind in their versions from before public corrections. In all three, the kit found the published error at the step that the correction names, together with further problems that we confirmed by hand. Given the same papers directly, the same language model working with Lean classified fewer results correctly on the longest paper and reported some statements narrower than the paper's as proved; no verdict of the kit claimed more than its Lean evidence showed.

item.title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
item.dc:creator: Per Kristian Lehre
item.description:
LLM agents design black-box optimisation algorithms and prove expected-runtime drift bounds in Lean, with Lean guards filtering flawed designs.
LLMs now prove hard theorems in Lean. Can they also design algorithms and prove their correctness and efficiency? LLM-guided design of optimisation heuristics (such as AlphaEvolve) is purely empirical. Automated theorem provers with LLMs prove given statements. So far, there has been little evidence that LLMs can do both: design an algorithm and guarantee its efficiency by a mathematical proof. We present a staged pipeline modelled after research methodology in design and analysis of evolutionary algorithms. The agent proposes black-box optimisation algorithms, and Lean guards filter out flawed designs. The agent then defines a potential function and proves drift bounds that guarantee an expected runtime improvement over the baseline algorithm. At no point in the pipeline are the algorithms compared empirically. The agent generates a black-box optimisation algorithm with expected runtime $O(n^2)$ on a CycleUncover problem, where the classical (1+1) EA needs runtime $e^{Ω(n)}$. The pipeline also designs and analyses a black-box optimisation algorithm for integer-valued submodular minimisation with expected runtime $O(n^{2+2c})$, and it matches the classical runtime $O(n^2)$ on LeadingOnes. Across 8 problem classes, 12 of 15 runs with frontier models complete the pipeline with a machine-checked expected-runtime bound. An ablation study shows that removing the staging and asking the agent to zero-shot an algorithmic design with a runtime guarantee leads to a copy of the seeded baseline algorithm (random search) or to incomplete proofs. Our study suggests that machine-checked specifications in Lean can replace empirical evaluation in open-ended algorithm discovery. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first example of an automated pipeline that designs efficient black-box optimisation algorithms with machine-checked runtime bounds in Lean.

item.title: MechAlign: Evaluating Semantic Alignment at the Project Level in Mathematical Formalization
item.dc:creator: Hao Shen, Ruichen Qiu, Lihong Zhi, Xiao-Shan Gao
item.description:
Builds LeanTrace, which extracts statement dependency graphs from elaborated Lean 4 declarations, enabling LLM review of semantic alignment and a benchmark from Lean projects.
Lean verifies that a formal proof establishes its stated proposition under declared assumptions, but does not check whether that proposition faithfully expresses the mathematical claim in a manuscript. Assessing this correspondence requires interpreting the main theorem through its project dependencies, which may be scattered throughout a large development. We introduce MechAlign, a framework for project-level semantic alignment review that combines formal dependency extraction with LLM-based assessment. Its extraction tool, LeanTrace, constructs a statement dependency graph from elaborated declarations, retaining definition bodies and structure constraints while excluding proof bodies and stopping at an explicit library boundary. The reviewer uses this context to investigate alignment and report discrepancies with localized evidence. We conduct a preliminary review of 201 main results from 173 OpenAI Math projects, using supplied informal descriptions and available paper context. A hyperbolic-group case illustrates how dependency inspection localizes a missing dimensional constraint relative to the manuscript, consistent with the upstream declaration of formalization scope. We also construct LeanReviewBench, comprising 501 fixed claim-statement-context triples from OpenAI Math, Fermat's Last Theorem, and Kakeya, with description provenance recorded. The resource supports controlled comparisons of more project-level semantic alignment evaluations.

item.title: Rainbow maps and the number of graceful labelings of trees
item.dc:creator: Shisheng Li
item.description:
The main asymptotic theorem is formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, provided as ancillary files. The combinatorial half is axiom-free and two Gamma-function identities are taken as axioms.
Let $τ(N)$ be the number of graceful labelings of trees with $N$ edges, that is, the number of spanning trees of the complete graph on $\{0,1,\dots,N\}$ whose edges have distinct lengths. The answer to exercise 7.2.2.3-106 of The Art of Computer Programming states that, if an empirical observation of Anick is true, then $τ(n)=\exp(n\ln n-n\ln(e/b)+O(\log n))$ with $b\approx0.636$, and that rigorous proofs are unknown. We prove that $|\logτ(N)-(N\log N-N\log(e/b))|\le152(1+\log(N+1))^4$ for every $N\ge3$, with $b=2/π$. A rainbow map of order $N$ sends each vertex $k\in\{1,\dots,N-1\}$ to a vertex $f(k)\in\{0,\dots,N\}$ so that the lengths $|f(k)-k|$ are $1,\dots,N-1$ in some order. Acyclic rainbow maps are exactly the graceful labelings, and all rainbow maps are counted by the Whitty numbers $W(N)$ (OEIS A134983). We show that $τ(N)\le W(N)\leτ(N)e^{151(1+\log(N+1))^4}$ by a combinatorial argument: for fixed directions, rainbow maps are rook placements on a Ferrers board; a swap injection shows that a uniformly random rainbow map has $O(\log^2N)$ cycles on average; and an inequality on the periods of a word shows that the $c$ cycles of a rainbow map can be removed by changing $O(c\log N)$ edges. We also show that $W(N)$ is the total weight of a family of weighted Motzkin paths. This yields exact enumerations, an alternating sum for $W(N)$, and a representation of $W(N)$ as a moment of a continuous dual Hahn weight, from which $|\log W(N)-(N\log(2N/π)-N)|\le5(1+\log(N+1))$. The main theorem has been formalized in Lean 4; its combinatorial half uses no axioms beyond those of Lean.

item.title: When is greedy exact for weighted minimum 3-cut?
item.dc:creator: Armando Rodado Amaris
item.description:
Formalizes the greedy-exactness theorem, the 4/3 bound, the merge lemmas, and a 7-vertex counterexample (checked by kernel evaluation) in Lean 4.
The greedy algorithm for minimum 3-cut splits a global minimum-weight cut and then the cheaper of its two sides; it is a tight $4/3$-approximation. We show that it is exact, from every global minimum-weight cut, whenever some optimal 3-partition has two parts joined by total weight at least the weighted edge connectivity $λ$. This extends both theorems of Hochbaum and Shmoys from unweighted planar graphs to all weighted graphs, recovers the $4/3$ bound, and generalizes to minimum $k$-cut with a one-paragraph proof. The remaining hard instances have all pair weights below $λ$; for them we prove a merge lemma for Gomory-Hu sides. Finally, we give a 7-vertex graph with a unique Gomory-Hu tree whose unique optimal 3-partition contains no side of that tree, so the first stage of Kapoor's algorithm does not suffice on its own. The main theorem, the 4/3 bound, the merge lemmas and the counterexample are verified in the Lean 4 proof assistant.

item.title: Bounds for the univalent Bloch-Landau constant
item.dc:creator: Frank Wikström
item.description:
A Lean 4 formalization, using Mathlib's exponential and logarithm bounds, proves the analytic bound U ≥ 0.592 with the Grunsky and Fekete–Szegő inequalities as hypotheses.
The univalent Bloch-Landau constant $\mathcal{U}$ is the largest number such that, for every univalent function $f$ on the unit disk, $f(\mathbb{D})$ contains a disk of radius $\mathcal{U} |f'(0)|$. We prove $0.612242\le\mathcal{U}<0.6562681$. The previous lower bound, $0.57088586$, came from growth estimates, which control disks centered at $f(0)$. Our improvement rests on a different mechanism. After Landau's normalization, a $2\times2$ compression of the Grunsky matrix constrains every omitted value through the same two coefficients, and choosing the center of the disk from these coefficients exploits this shared information. A short analytic proof based on this idea gives $\mathcal{U}\ge0.592$; it has been formalized in Lean, with the classical Grunsky and Fekete-Szegő inequalities as the only external inputs. Retaining complex quadratic forms of the matrix gives $\mathcal{U}\ge0.612242$ through a finite interval certificate, and this bound holds for every normalized univalent function with $a_2=0$ and $|a_3|\le1/3$. We also show that no argument based on disks centered at $f(0)$ can give a bound above $0.6$. For the upper bound we construct an explicit domain, bounded by Goodman's first two slit generations, thirty analytic arcs and a circle. We certify $\mathcal{U}<0.6562681$ with a capacity estimate for almost critical arcs, improving the best published bound $0.6563937$.

item.title: Efficient Proof Generation for Lean Statements with Multiple Candidate Answers
item.dc:creator: Pengzhen Lin, Ke Zhang, Maziar Raissi, Zhouxing Shi
item.description:
Trains Lean 4 provers that select or propose candidate answers and prove them jointly in one call, verified by Lean 4.26.
In formal systems such as Lean 4, efficiently finding answers to mathematical problems and generating verifiable proofs is an important task in automated mathematical reasoning. In the traditional way where an upstream solver provides multiple candidate answers, the common workflow requires searching for proofs for each candidate separately, incurring redundant computational cost. To this end, we propose a joint proof framework that integrates candidate answer selection, answer supplementation, and formal proof generation into a unified reasoning process. At its core is a trained prover that selects given or proposes new answers and generates a proof for at least one answer in a single call. Joint proof can also reuse generated proofs to check for faithfulness errors. For problems with a unique answer, if two distinct answers both obtain verifiable proofs under the same formal statement, this confirms the statement does not faithfully preserve the original problem semantics. On MATH-500, AMC 2023, and AIME 2024/2025/2026, our framework achieves the same formal proof success rate as per-candidate proof generation with about one sixth of the token cost, and identifies at least 6.1% of the formalized statements as unfaithful without requiring additional judges. Our model and code are available at https://github.com/Linppz/Gobble-Prover.

item.title: Speculative Decoding for Mixture-of-Experts Models: Expert Bytes, Kernel Bandwidth and the Best Draft Length
item.dc:creator: Yuzheng Lan
item.description:
Theorems on when speculative decoding beats plain decoding, the optimal draft length, and bandwidth-error bounds are proved in Lean 4 against Mathlib (package MoESpec).
Speculative decoding checks several drafted tokens in one verification pass. On a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, consecutive tokens often select the same experts. A deduplicating engine reads each selected expert once per pass, so it requests fewer bytes than a per-slot engine, which reads it once per token. We write a step's time as the bytes each kernel requests over its effective bandwidth, plus fixed time. Under geometric acceptance, we derive from this step time when speculation is faster than plain decoding. The best draft length is a monotone staircase in the acceptance rate. We bound how a bandwidth error moves each result, and we check the main steps in Lean. Deduplication is faster exactly where its share $\bar u(n)$ of the per-slot bytes is below its ratio $r(n)$ of the per-slot bandwidth. On llama.cpp Metal, MLX-LM and llama.cpp CUDA, which we modified to deduplicate, the per-slot kernel has the higher effective bandwidth (r = 0.32 to 0.75). Thus deduplication is faster only from 5 to 8 tokens per pass, or never. We fit the bandwidths on one layer's expert operation, run alone, in under an hour per model. Bytes from routing traces over these bandwidths predict the time that deduplication saves. The measured saving lies inside its error bound at every point on CUDA and MLX-LM and at 36 of 48 points on Metal. The crossover is the first pass size at which deduplication is faster. The prediction places it within one pass size in 10 of 12 configurations of engine, model and depth. We computed these predictions after the measurements. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, operation times measured before its speculative runs give the best draft length on CUDA within one at all 22 acceptance values.

item.title: PastaLean: Deterministic transpilation from Python to Lean for Verification
item.dc:creator: Anirudh Gupta, Petros Markopoulos, Siddhartha Gadgil
item.description:
Transpiles Python into shallow Lean 4 embeddings via Lean metaprogramming, producing a provable twin with contract theorems and a runnable twin for execution.
We present PastaLean, an extensible system for deterministic translation from Python to Lean via the Abstract Syntax Tree of Python. This allows for verification of Python code, especially auxiliary code used by AI. Every program is translated into a provable twin written in the form Lean's verification tooling can reason about, and a runnable twin that gives a fast and correct computation support. We also introduce our Type Inference engine TypeInfer which provides static typing support for untyped Python code. Our tool provides coverage of more than 92% for LeetCode and HumanEval\textsuperscript{+} and more than 98% for LiveCodeBench ground truth Python files. Further, at least 97% of each dataset's (numerical) test cases pass, with 100% on HumanEval\textsuperscript{+} and LiveCodeBench. The TypeInfer engine is the best-scoring tool on the TypeEvalPy static leaderboard, and on a repository-level TypyBench benchmark it scores above every competing repository-level inference tool.

item.title: BFGS can converge to non-Clarke-stationary points with positive probability
item.dc:creator: Lexiao Lai
item.description:
The main result, that BFGS converges to a non-Clarke-stationary point, is formalized in Lean in an accompanying GitHub repository.
We construct a coercive, locally Lipschitz, semialgebraic function on $\mathbb R^2$ for which BFGS with Armijo–Wolfe line search converges to a non-Clarke-stationary point from a nonempty open set of initial points and inverse-Hessian estimates. This disproves the almost-sure stationarity assertion in the 2013 challenge of Lewis and Overton. The construction and proof combine analytical arguments with computer-assisted verification of explicit inequalities.

item.title: Numina Fuse: Interactive Autoformalization in Lean 4
item.dc:creator: Justin Asher, Yichuan Cao, Ruichen Qiu, Pietro Pellegrino, Jia Li
item.description:
Builds an agent-based application for autoformalization of mathematics in Lean 4 with blueprints, and evaluates LLM prover models on Lean lemmas.
Numina Fuse is an agent-native application for formalizing mathematics in Lean 4. Since Lean can compile while not representing its intended informal meaning, and agents now write Lean faster than people can read it, we built Fuse around human supervision of agent work. A user works with an AI orchestrator on a Lean project and supervises it through views of the blueprint, the dependency graph, and the Lean code, while the backend keeps the project's derived state and runs agents for hours without the user present. We describe the development of Fuse throughout 2026, as it moved from a prescribed pipeline of agents paced by human review to an orchestrator that dispatches specialists, provers, and parallel children on its own. We designed for this shift, keeping project state, tooling, and interface design separate from orchestration so that agents could take over more of the work as models improved. We report Fuse's use in a formalization of the three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture and a study of prover models. We close with lessons for the next generation of autoformalization systems. Fuse Desktop, an open-source local version, is available at https://github.com/project-numina/fuse-desktop.

item.title: Coordinate systems and maximal order complexity in Banach lattices
item.dc:creator: A. Avilés, C. Rosendal, M. A. Taylor, P. Tradacete
item.description:
The paper's results on order bases and coanalytic complexity in Banach lattices are formalized in Lean 4 using Mathlib and the BanLat library, with LLM assistance.
We resolve three questions arising from the study of coordinate systems and order convergence in Banach lattices. Firstly, every order (respectively, $σ$-order) basis $(e_n)$ for a Banach lattice $X=[e_n]$ is automatically a Schauder basis. In fact, the associated partial sum projections satisfy a maximal inequality, and hence every such basis is uniform. Secondly, we show that there is a separable Banach lattice $X$ in which the set $$ X_{\downarrow0}=\{(x_n)\in X^{\mathbb N}:x_1\geqslant x_2\geqslant\ldots\geqslant 0=\inf_nx_n\} $$ is $\mathbfΠ^1_1$-complete. Finally, we construct a separable Banach lattice $Y$ for which the set $Y^{\uparrow\infty}$ of increasing positive sequences which are not order bounded is $\mathbfΠ^1_1$-complete. It follows that neither $X_{\downarrow0}$ nor $Y^{\uparrow\infty}$ can be described in any simpler way than by the nonexistence of positive lower and upper bounds, respectively.

item.title: The Cost of an Unknown Horizon for the Last Iterate of Clipped SGD under Heavy-Tailed Noise
item.dc:creator: Yuxing Peng, Zhiqing Tang, Weijia Jia
item.description:
Lean 4 with Mathlib machine-checks the lower bounds (Theorems 5 and 11(i)) and the known-horizon last-iterate bound for clipped SGD.
Training is often stopped at a data-dependent time, so guarantees for the last iterate must hold at all times simultaneously. We determine the optimal time-uniform rate for the last iterate of clipped SGD on smooth convex objectives under heavy-tailed noise with a bounded central $p$th moment, $1<p\le2$. A schedule without horizon or confidence inputs attains $\tilde O(t^{-β_p})$ at all times, with $β_p=2(p-1)/(3p-1)$, also almost surely, and no rule that steps along the stochastic gradient at its current iterate attains $\tilde O(t^{-r})$ for any $r>β_p$, even with adaptive step sizes and thresholds. This rate lies between the optimal rate $O(T^{-α_p})$ for a known horizon $T$, $α_p=(p-1)/p$, and the previous time-uniform rate $\tilde O(t^{-2(p-1)/(3p)})$ (Chezhegov et al., ICLR 2026); under finite variance, the exponents are $1/2$, $2/5$, and $1/3$. Their conjecture that a better schedule reaches the optimal rate thus holds with a known horizon (Liu; Jiang et al.) but fails without one. Querying gradients at the running average attains $\tilde O(t^{-α_p})$ at all times, whereas heavy-ball momentum with geometric forgetting and polynomially bounded steps cannot improve on $β_p$.

item.title: Formalising John Dee's Monas Hieroglyphica in Lean 4
item.dc:creator: Ivan Matychyn
item.description:
Formalises the theorems of John Dee's Monas Hieroglyphica in Lean 4 core (no Mathlib), including a constructive proof that the cube root of 2 is irrational.
John Dee's Monas Hieroglyphica (Antwerp, 1564) contains twenty-four numbered theorems about a single composite alchemical glyph, presented in the manner of Euclid: theorem, demonstration, corollary. In this note the following question is considered: which of Dee's theorems can be stated precisely in a proof assistant, and which of them can then be proved? Working in Lean 4 (v4.35.0) with the core library only (without Mathlib), we divide the treatise into three layers: the syntax of the glyph, encoded as inductive data; Dee's arithmetic, verified by kernel computation; and the geometry of the final theorems, in connection with which we prove a classical result not stated by Dee: no ratio of whole numbers doubles the cube, that is, the cube root of two is irrational (the Delian obstruction). The accompanying file Monas.lean compiles with no errors and no sorry. Two observations are made. The cabalistic computation of Theorem XVII, according to which the Cross, "by the best kabbalistic computation," signifies the number 252, is verified, and its proof depends on no axioms: it is a pure computation. The only theorem of the formalisation with genuine mathematical content, the Delian obstruction, is proved constructively and depends only on the axioms propext and Quot.sound.

item.title: SemantEq: Faithful Bidirectional Equivalence of Formal Statements
item.dc:creator: Xinrui Li, Pawan Sasanka Ammanamanchi, Siddharth Bhat, Rianna Jamdar, Yongxi Lin, Stella Biderman
item.description:
Implements a deterministic Lean 4 metaprogram and a proof-term auditor that judge equivalence of autoformalized Mathlib statements on ProofNetVerif.
Statement autoformalization translates mathematics from natural language into a proof assistant such as Lean 4, and models now do it at scale. As provers get stronger, the burden of correctness shifts from the proof to the statement, that is, to whether the formal statement faithfully translates its source. Given a trusted reference formalization, the natural test is logical equivalence, and it proves too much. $P \leftrightarrow Q$ holds trivially for any two statements $P$ and $Q$ that the library proves, because a prover can prove each separately and pass through $P \leftrightarrow \mathrm{True} \leftrightarrow Q$. The stronger the prover, the more unrelated pairs pass. Earlier methods restrict the prover and check that each proof names the other statement. We introduce SemantEq, a more principled relation that instead requires each statement to turn into the other only through a chain of allowed steps, such as logical rearrangement and rewriting with the library's own equations. Our programs judge a proof by the proof term Lean checks, not by its tactic script. SemantEq-Eval, a search without a model, reaches 100% precision and 65.6% recall on the ProofNetVerif test split under our adjudicated labels, against 95.8% and 61.8% for BEq+, and an 8.9-fold increase in its CPU time adds at most three pairs. A language model finds more proofs, but under two of four prompts it proves both directions of about two in five of the non-equivalent pairs. SemantEq-ProofAudit audits each model-written proof under a policy derived from the relation and accepts none of the 104 non-equivalent pairs, and it raises recall on 407 equivalent pairs from 65.4% to 81.1% under the best prompt. Separating the generation of equivalence proofs from their acceptance lets a stronger prover raise recall without changing what an acceptance means. We release code and data at: https://github.com/hlxr89/SemantEq

item.title: Sharp Bounds on the Winner's Bias under Independent and Nonnegatively Correlated Noise
item.dc:creator: Ivan Viakhirev, Kirill Borodin, Grach Mkrtchian
item.description:
All theorems, corollaries and lemmas on sharp winner's-bias constants are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib, in about 7,900 lines with no sorry.
Reporting the best of $M$ noisy, unbiased scores overstates the winner's value by up to $c\sqrt{V}$, where $V$ is the total noise variance and the sharp constant $c$ depends on how the noise is dependent. It was known only at the two extremes, arbitrary dependence ($\sqrt{(M-1)/M}$) and i.i.d. noise. We determine it for two classes in between: for independent, not identically distributed noise it is $\sqrt{(M-1)/(2M)}$, and for pairwise nonnegatively correlated noise it is $(M-1)/M$; for uncorrelated noise this answers the maximum version of an open question about the expected range. Explicit finite constructions attain both. As a corollary, the bias of the cross-validation estimator is bounded sharply within each class. All theorems are formally verified in Lean 4. Across 448 language-model and classifier selection pipelines, designs with per-candidate items realize a median 0.75 of the independent-class ceiling. At a fixed item budget, scoring all candidates on shared items is markedly less optimistic than giving each candidate its own items.

item.title: A frame-indifferent rank-one convex function in three dimensions which is not quasiconvex
item.dc:creator: Sergio Conti, Georg Dolzmann, Patrick Dondl
item.description:
The main theorems (1.1 and 2.1) were formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib. The formalization was written entirely by Claude Opus 5.5 under author guidance.
We construct a function $W:\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}\to\mathbb{R}$ which is frame-indifferent, $W(QF)=W(F)$ for all $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$, rank-one convex, but not quasiconvex. In a neighbourhood of $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ the function is an explicit polynomial of degree four in the strain $F^TF-\mathrm{Id}$; the failure of quasiconvexity occurs at $F=\mathrm{Id}$ through a third-order mechanism of Šverák type, with test functions whose gradients are arbitrarily close to $\mathrm{Id}$. The polynomial is obtained from a geometrically linear example, a rank-one convex, non-quasiconvex quartic polynomial of the symmetric part of the gradient, by evaluating it at the strain $\frac12(F^TF-\mathrm{Id})$, adding a uniaxial prestress and a cubic correction, and enlarging the quartic term. The local function is extended to all of $\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ by adding a frame-indifferent polyconvex function which vanishes near $\mathrm{SO}(3)$. This work was carried out with the assistance of the AI model Claude Opus 5.5; the proofs of the main results have been formally verified in Lean 4.

item.title: PaperFormalizer: Author-in-the-Loop Autoformalization of Research Papers in Lean
item.dc:creator: Jiyuan Tan, Jose Blanchet, Vasilis Syrgkanis
item.description:
Agentic pipeline that autoformalizes research papers into Lean against Mathlib and domain libraries, with author-in-the-loop review and repair.
Even a carefully proofread paper can leave small gaps in its proofs or its stated assumptions. We introduce PaperFormalizer, a Lean-based agentic pipeline that helps authors find and close such gaps in their own papers and turn each paper into a Lean-verified version. Starting from the LaTeX source, PaperFormalizer transcribes the paper into a dependency graph of statements, audits each statement in natural language for faithfulness, ambiguity and correctness, and then formalizes and proves the statements in Lean against Mathlib, optional domain libraries and the author's personal toolkit. Only the author knows what a statement is meant to say and how a formalization gap in a result is best fixed. The pipeline therefore stops and asks the author whenever a statement admits more than one reading, presents every repair, in natural language and TeX symbols, as a proposal that the author can accept, decline or redirect, and leaves to the author every decision that could potentially change what the paper claims. The output is an annotated and revised version of the paper, a report of the changes, and Lean code in which each declaration is linked to the statement it formalizes. The author's toolkit grows as more papers are formalized, and authors can share their verified papers so that researchers who build on them can reuse their Lean code. By making verified papers practical to produce, PaperFormalizer aims to make research that rests on mathematical proofs more robust. PaperFormalizer runs inside a coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) and is available at https://github.com/Jiyuan-Tan/PaperFormalizer. Papers with Lean code shared by users are available at https://paperformalizer.org.

item.title: Verified Pauli-Product Measurement Compilation for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation
item.dc:creator: John Zhuoyang Ye, Jens Palsberg
item.description:
Mechanizes QPPM semantics, Hoare logic, verified lowering and optimization, and approximation bounds in Lean with Mathlib, and uses Lean kernel-checked certificates on benchmarks.
Fault-tolerant quantum compilers implement gates through Pauli-product measurements and classical feedback. Verifying such a compiler requires reasoning about the quantum state and the recorded outcomes together: a correction reads an outcome, a gate's internal outcomes must be hidden from its caller, and an application's outcomes must survive optimization. We introduce QPPM, a language for Pauli-product measurement programs, with a weakest-precondition semantics over store-indexed matrix assertions, following quantum Hoare logic with classical variables. Every program terminates, so the Hoare logic is a syntactic presentation of weakest preconditions whose soundness and relative completeness are immediate. Its value is that component specifications compose. All results are mechanized in Lean. We verify lowering of Clifford+$T$ circuits to QPPM with private outcomes and supplied magic states, and an optimizer that eliminates measurements, fuses and reorders rotations, and schedules logical rounds while preserving every outcome that subsequent code can read. A compositional approximation relation bounds the effect of synthesis error on specifications and on output trace distance, and a certificate-checked pipeline selects, among synthesized circuits that meet the user's error limit, the one with the lowest certified depth bound. On QASMBench, verified fusion and scheduling reduce logical measurement depth by a median of 17.9%, and complete source-to-QPPM allowances are certified for all 35 valid selected small-suite inputs.

item.title: Finite Mass Response to Vanishing Perturbations at Cauchy Horizons
item.dc:creator: Yi-kun Li
item.description:
The paper's mathematical results and proofs on mass response at Cauchy horizons are formalized in Lean 4, with a public repository and verification instructions.
Smooth transverse perturbations with vanishing $L^p$ norm, for fixed finite $p\ge4$, can leave a finite positive mass increment at a Cauchy horizon. We prove this at a critical surface-gravity relation in the spherical Einstein–Maxwell–scalar system with positive cosmological constant. Each solution has bounded mass and local finite-energy weak extensions. The response escapes every fixed time window. An analytic law determines its delay and duration, and resolves enhancement or cancellation for overlapping packets.

item.title: On the proof of the Kozma-Nitzan conjecture
item.dc:creator: Jean-Baptiste Gouéré
item.description:
Cites a third-party Lean 4/Mathlib formalization of θ(p_c)=0 for Bernoulli bond percolation on Z^d, the result the exposition concerns.
In this short note, we give an exposition of the recent proof of the Kozma-Nitzan conjecture provided by OpenAI.

item.title: Hitting time for loose Hamilton cycles in the random hypergraph process
item.dc:creator: Jared León, Xizhi Liu
item.description:
Provides a Lean 4 formalisation, produced largely by an LLM, of the hitting-time theorem for loose Hamilton cycles in r-uniform hypergraphs with (r-1)|n.
The random hypergraph process starts with an empty hypergraph on $n$ vertices and adds a uniformly chosen missing edge at each step. For even $n$, we prove that, with high probability, a $3$-uniform loose Hamilton cycle appears when the last isolated vertex disappears. The approach developed here adapts arguments from Kahn's work on perfect matchings. It can also be extended to obtain the corresponding hitting-time theorems for $r=2$ and every fixed $r\ge4$ satisfying $(r-1)\mid n$. Furthermore, it can be used to estimate the numbers of loose Hamilton cycles at these hitting times for every fixed $r\ge2$, up to a factor of $\exp\{o(n)\}$.

item.title: AssureCode: Structured Justification for Trustworthy Agentic Coding
item.dc:creator: Logan Murphy, Wilson Sy, Rhys Balevicius, Kelsie Fung, Karenna Kung, Aren A. Babikian, Marsha Chechik
item.description:
Uses Lean as the formalization backend and theorem prover for autoformalized intent specifications, decomposition-soundness proofs, and test-oracle alignment checks in agentic coding.
The use of AI-based tools in software development is rapidly changing how software is produced, enabling large volumes of code to be generated with limited human implementation effort. However, this raises fundamental challenges for ensuring that generated artifacts are aligned with developer intent and have been appropriately validated. In this work, we propose the use of structured argumentation in driving AI-assisted software development. Inspired by techniques from assurance engineering for safety-critical systems, we define a language of justification rationales that explicitly relate informal natural language prompts, formal specifications, assumptions about developer intentions, and program analysis evidence in a structured and verifiable format. We then describe AssureCode, a tool-supported methodology for creating such rationales as part of agentic code generation. We provide an empirical analysis of our implementation where we investigate its capacity to contribute towards justified assurance of correctness for AI-generated code.

item.title: Residue Sums Modulo Products of Two Distinct Odd Primes
item.dc:creator: Haobo Ma, Mircea Merca, Wenlin Zhang
item.description:
Lean 4 formalizations, with a pinned public repository, verify a counterexample to Merca's Conjecture 1 and prove his lifted prime-modulus residue-sum Conjecture 2.
Let $S_m(a)$ denote the sum of the least positive residues in one multiplicative period of $a$ modulo $m$, of length $k$. We study the equality $S_m(a)=mk/2$ for $m=pq$, where $p,q$ are distinct odd primes and $k$ is even. Complementary pairing settles subgroups containing $-1$; the remaining cases depend on their embedding in the two local unit groups. At index four, we exclude mixed cyclic subgroups with biquadratic annihilator and classify every eligible imprimitive quartic kernel using two odd integer moments at its prime conductor. For each fixed conductor, the proportion of admissible second primes giving equality is $1/4$ or $1/2$; full coset balance has proportion $1/4$. For primitive quartic characters, classical triangular character-sum identities yield explicit short-sum criteria, and the relative class-number formula gives an obstruction to a centered coset. At index six, we give structural counts and construct an infinite family modulo $19q$ in which nonzero sextic and quadratic moments cancel. These applications use a standard odd-character expansion, which also recovers the known index-two balance classification and determines the sign of its deviation. A reproducible census for $pq\le10000$ counts $75\,090$ eligible cyclic subgroups and identifies $101$ mixed index-four subgroups whose own sum is centered although some coset sums are not.

item.title: When Do Gaussian Priors Fail? A Latent Geometry Investigation of RL Fine-Tuning
item.dc:creator: Wang Ru
item.description:
Lean 4 with Mathlib machine-checks the algebraic skeleton of the paper's theory, including the width-center formula, the crossover identity and the limit claims.
Latent diffusion models almost universally place a Gaussian prior on the VAE latent space. For base generation this default is unproblematic; under reinforcement-learning fine-tuning, however, it carries a structural limitation. The standard VAE's KL term does not merely ignore mode structure - it actively taxes separation and tightness. When data are multimodal, the ELBO optimum compresses distinct modes into an overlapping latent. RL fine-tuning amplifies this overlap: the score network is under-resolved on the saddle region between modes, dynamic-to-variational amplification rises sharply, and the collapse boundary beta_c is pushed far above its variational scale. On the real alanine-dipeptide Boltzmann distribution, a Gaussian-prior VAE collapses at beta_c = 0.224 while a mode-tracked Gaussian-mixture prior collapses at 0.00316, a 71x gap from the same pipeline. We trace this gap to a single geometric mediator, d_min/(2 sigma_0), and verify the causal chain through controlled interventions: moving geometry at fixed prior, and switching prior at matched geometry (full mediation; prior-label coefficient 0.995x, 95% CI [0.79, 1.25]). A three-source decomposition localises the amplification to the learned policy (zero ODE-solver contribution, bounded anchor mismatch); the coverage plateau is an unconditional benefit of mode-separating priors that no amount of RL capacity recovers. The remedy is conditional: a non-Gaussian prior is necessary precisely when the latent geometry would fall into overlap and the task is coverage-sensitive. A machine-checked theory skeleton supports the KL pricing structure - a divergent compactness tax under a Gaussian prior versus a finite assignment fee under a mixture - and the position-versus-plateau distinction delimits what is finite-resource from what requires changing the prior.

item.title: Thin-Layer Dichotomy in Three-Phase Mullins-Sekerka Flow: Gap Dynamics and Composite Interfaces
item.dc:creator: Tokuhiro Eto
item.description:
Selected results on the fixed-mode linearized Mullins–Sekerka system were formalized in Lean 4, with AI assistants helping develop the formalization.
We study the thin-layer limit of the Mullins-Sekerka flow in concentric circular geometries at fixed wave number $k$, contrasting a two-phase annulus with a genuine three-phase layer. A dichotomy emerges: for $k\ge2$ the rates blow up like the inverse thickness when the same phase lies on both sides of the layer, whereas between two different phases the matrix governing the linearized Fourier mode extends analytically to zero thickness. Both cases share the singular Dirichlet-to-Neumann factor of the thin annulus and differ only in whether the Gibbs-Thomson law forces an order-one potential difference across it. In the three-phase case the pure thickness-modulation rate stays below the logarithmic growth rate of the mean thickness, for every $k\ge1$ and all positive tensions, and, after projection onto the mean displacement and the outer interface, the collapsed pair moves as one interface carrying the sum of the two tensions. All statements concern the instantaneous fixed-mode linearization. The singularity is a property of the phase coupling, not of the thin geometry.

item.title: Can Reciprocal RIS Perform as Non-Reciprocal RIS?
item.dc:creator: Matteo Nerini, Juan Vidal Alegría, Bruno Clerckx
item.description:
